svg.text: Reading a full blood count: the indices tell you the cause
MCV — average red cell size
LIKELY CAUSE IN GHANA
LOW — microcytic, under 80 fL
Iron deficiency, thalassaemia, chronic blood loss
NORMAL — normocytic, 80 to 100
Acute bleeding, chronic disease, haemolysis, malaria
HIGH — macrocytic, over 100 fL
B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease
Hookworm and heavy menstrual loss are the commonest reasons a Ghanaian adult is microcytic.
White cell differential
NEUTROPHILS up — bacterial infection
LYMPHOCYTES up — viral infection, TB
EOSINOPHILS up — parasites, allergy
Very common in Ghana: worms, schistosomiasis
NEUTROPHILS under 1.0 — the patient
cannot mount pus. Fever alone is an emergency.
Results that must be phoned, not filed
Potassium under 2.5 or over 6.5
Glucose under 2.5 or very high with ketones
Haemoglobin under 7 g/dL
Platelets under 20
Any positive blood culture
Read it back. Record who you told and when.
Before you believe a result, ask whether the sample was any good
A potassium of 6.8 in a well patient with a normal ECG is far more likely haemolysis than hyperkalaemia.
A sample taken from the arm with the drip running measures the drip, not the patient.
A glucose taken hours ago and left standing reads falsely low — the cells keep consuming it.
Repeat the sample when the result and the patient disagree. Never treat a number you do not believe,
and never ignore one either. Repeat it, and treat the patient in front of you meanwhile.
The quality of the specimen sets the ceiling on the result.
